## 1. Load the processed data

```{r load}
# Open the project's .Rproj file before running chunks.
# Install psych once in the Console if needed: install.packages("psych")

install.packages("psych")
library(psych)

h1 <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv")
h2 <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv")

```

## 2. Look at the distribution first

```{r histogram}
# A histogram groups numerical values into intervals (bins).
# Bar height shows how many observations fall in each interval.
# Start by looking at the distribution before calculating summary statistics.

hist(h1$self_physatt)
# hist(h1$cot_politics) # does not work because categoric variable
hist(h2$attract_importance_1)
hist(h2$app_enh_total)


# Add readable labels to histograms.
hist(h1$self_physatt,
     main = "Distribution of Physical Attractivness",
     xlab = "Self-Rated Physical Attractivness (1-10)")

hist(h2$attract_importance_1,
     main = "Distribution of Importance of Own Attractivness",
     xlab = "Self-Rated of Importance of Own Attractivness (1-9)")

hist(h2$app_enh_total,
     main = "Time Spent Enhancing Appearance",
     xlab = "Sum of Composite measure of Enhancing Own Appearance (in min)")

```

## 3. One statistic at a time

```{r individual_statistics}
# Mean: add the scores and divide by the number of observed responses.
sum(is.na(h1$self_physatt)) # 0
sum(is.na(h1$cot_politics)) # 0
sum(is.na(h2$attract_importance_1)) # 0
sum(is.na(h2$app_enh_total)) # 0
# no NAs in all our data
mean(h1$self_physatt) # 6.777964
mean(h2$attract_importance_1) # 7.384656
mean(h2$app_enh_total) # 574.458

# Median: the middle score after sorting the responses.
median(h1$self_physatt) # 6
median(h2$attract_importance_1) # 7
median(h2$app_enh_total) # 420

# Table: count how many people are in each category.
table(h1$cot_politics)
#      center  center_left center_right     far_left    far_right 
#      34842        26063        11848         8083         2308 

# Range: return the minimum and maximum, rather than their difference.
range(h1$self_physatt) # 1 11
range(h2$attract_importance_1) # 1 9
range(h2$app_enh_total) # 0 2880

# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile.
IQR(h1$self_physatt) # 2
IQR(h2$attract_importance_1) # 2
IQR(h2$app_enh_total) # 291

```

## 4. Standardize a variable

```{r standardize}
# scale() uses z = (original score - mean) / standard deviation by default.
# Keep the original commitment scores and store the standardized values separately.
# scale() returns a matrix; as.numeric() makes a simple numeric column.

h1$self_physatt_z <- scale(h1$self_physatt) 
h2$attract_importance_1_z <- scale(h2$attract_importance_1)
h2$app_enh_total_z <- scale(h2$app_enh_total) 

# Standardized scores have mean approximately 0 and standard deviation 1.
round(mean(h1$self_physatt_z), digits = 5) # 0
round(mean(h2$attract_importance_1_z), digits = 5) # 0
round(mean(h2$app_enh_total_z), digits = 5) # 0

round(sd(h1$self_physatt_z), digits = 5) # 1
round(sd(h2$attract_importance_1_z), digits = 5) # 1
round(sd(h2$app_enh_total_z), digits = 5) # 1

# show hist
hist(h1$self_physatt_z)
hist(h2$attract_importance_1_z)
hist(h2$app_enh_total_z)

```

## 5. Covariance and correlation

```{r association}
# Covariance describes whether two variables tend to move together.
# Positive: higher values tend to occur together. Negative: higher values tend to accompany lower values.
# Its size depends on the units and is not restricted to -1 through 1.
cov(h2$attract_importance_1, h2$app_enh_total, use = "complete.obs")
# use = "complete.obs" - only use when complete observations in both variables
# 96.68606

# Pearson correlation expresses a linear association on a -1 to 1 scale.
cor(h2$attract_importance_1, h2$app_enh_total, use = "complete.obs")
# 0.1288774
# slight positive associaton

# Select numerical variables only; do not include participant IDs or category codes.
cor_data <- h2[,c("attract_importance_1","app_enh_total")]

# A correlation matrix gives the correlation for each pair of columns.
# The diagonal is 1 because each variable is correlated with itself.
cor(cor_data, use = "complete.obs")
#                      attract_importance_1 app_enh_total
# attract_importance_1            1.0000000     0.1288774
# app_enh_total                   0.1288774     1.0000000

cor(h2[,c("attract_importance_1","app_enh_total")], use = "complete.obs")
# this works too without creating another df
#                      attract_importance_1 app_enh_total
# attract_importance_1            1.0000000     0.1288774
# app_enh_total                   0.1288774     1.0000000

```

## 6. Several statistics at once

```{r combined_summaries}
# summary() reports minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum, and missing counts when present.
summary(h1)
summary(h2)

# psych::describe() reports n, mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum, range width (max minus min), skewness, kurtosis, and other summaries.
psych::describe(h1)
psych::describe(h2)

# However it does not report every statistic above: compute IQR, cov(), and cor() separately.
```
